final_proof:
**Conventions and definitions.**

Throughout, $X$ is a set and $\mathcal P(X)$ is its power set. For a set $Z$, $\mathcal P(X)^Z$ is the set of all families $(A_z)_{z\in Z}$ of subsets of $X$ (that is, all maps $Z\to\mathcal P(X)$). For $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$, $\mathcal S^Z\subseteq\mathcal P(X)^Z$ is the set of families all of whose members lie in $\mathcal S$. In particular $\mathcal P(X)^{\varnothing}$ has exactly one element, the empty family $e$, and $e\in\mathcal S^{\varnothing}$ for every $\mathcal S$, including $\mathcal S=\varnothing$.

*Magma of sets.* Let $I$ be an index set, and for each $i\in I$ let $Z_i$ be a set and $\phi_i:\mathcal P(X)^{Z_i}\to\mathcal P(X)$ a mapping (an operation of arity $Z_i$ on subsets of $X$). A collection $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ is a *magma of sets for* $\{\phi_i: i\in I\}$ iff it is closed under every $\phi_i$:
$$\forall i\in I\ \ \forall (A_z)_{z\in Z_i}\in\mathcal S^{Z_i}:\quad \phi_i\big((A_z)_{z\in Z_i}\big)\in\mathcal S .$$

*$\sigma$-algebra.* A collection $\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $X$ iff
- (SA1) $X\in\Sigma$;
- (SA2) for all $A\in\Sigma$: $X\setminus A\in\Sigma$;
- (SA3) for every sequence $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$: $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\Sigma$.

**Claim.** There are an index set $I$ and operations $\phi_i$ ($i\in I$) on $\mathcal P(X)$ such that, for every $\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$,
$$\Sigma\text{ is a }\sigma\text{-algebra on }X\iff \Sigma\text{ is a magma of sets for }\{\phi_i:i\in I\}.$$
That is, the concept of $\sigma$-algebra is an instance of the concept of magma of sets.

**Construction.** Let $I=\{1,2,3\}$ and put $Z_1=\varnothing$, $Z_2=\{0\}$ (a one-element set), $Z_3=\mathbb N$. Define
- $\phi_1:\mathcal P(X)^{\varnothing}\to\mathcal P(X)$ by $\phi_1(e)=X$ (a nullary operation, i.e. a constant);
- $\phi_2:\mathcal P(X)^{\{0\}}\to\mathcal P(X)$ by $\phi_2\big((A_0)\big)=X\setminus A_0$;
- $\phi_3:\mathcal P(X)^{\mathbb N}\to\mathcal P(X)$ by $\phi_3\big((A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\big)=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n$.

These are well-defined mappings into $\mathcal P(X)$: $X\subseteq X$; $X\setminus A_0\subseteq X$; and a union of subsets of $X$ is a subset of $X$.

**Proof of the equivalence.** Fix $\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$. We show that closure of $\Sigma$ under $\phi_k$ is equivalent to (SA$k$), for $k=1,2,3$. Since $\Sigma$ is a magma of sets for $\{\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3\}$ iff it is closed under each of $\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3$, and $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-algebra iff (SA1), (SA2), (SA3) all hold, this proves the claim.

*$k=1$.* $\Sigma^{\varnothing}=\{e\}$, so closure under $\phi_1$ says exactly $\phi_1(e)\in\Sigma$, i.e. $X\in\Sigma$, which is (SA1).

*$k=2$.* The map $A\mapsto (A)$ (the family with the single member $A$ at index $0$) is a bijection from $\Sigma$ onto $\Sigma^{\{0\}}$. Hence closure under $\phi_2$, i.e. $\phi_2((A_0))\in\Sigma$ for all $(A_0)\in\Sigma^{\{0\}}$, says precisely that $X\setminus A\in\Sigma$ for all $A\in\Sigma$, which is (SA2).

*$k=3$.* $\Sigma^{\mathbb N}$ is exactly the set of sequences $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with every $A_n\in\Sigma$, and $\phi_3$ sends such a sequence to $\bigcup_n A_n$. So closure under $\phi_3$ is literally (SA3).

Thus $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $X$ if and only if $\Sigma$ is a magma of sets for $\{\phi_1,\phi_2,\phi_3\}$. $\blacksquare$

**Remarks on variant definitions (robustness).**

1. *"Countable unions" including finite families.* Some texts phrase (SA3) as closure under unions of arbitrary countable (finite or countably infinite) families. This is equivalent to (SA3) given (SA1), (SA2), so the same operations work. Indeed, (SA3) follows from the countable-family version by taking the family indexed by $\mathbb N$. Conversely, assume (SA1)-(SA3), and let $(A_j)_{j\in J}$ be a family in $\Sigma$ with $J$ countable. If $J=\varnothing$, the union is $\varnothing=X\setminus X\in\Sigma$ by (SA1), (SA2). If $J\neq\varnothing$, there is a surjection $s:\mathbb N\to J$ (because $J$ is countable and nonempty), and $\bigcup_{j\in J}A_j=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_{s(n)}\in\Sigma$ by (SA3), since every $j\in J$ equals $s(n)$ for some $n$.

2. *$\varnothing\in\Sigma$ instead of $X\in\Sigma$.* If a $\sigma$-algebra is defined with (SA1') $\varnothing\in\Sigma$ in place of (SA1), replace $\phi_1$ with $\phi_1'(e)=\varnothing$. The argument for $k=1$ goes through word for word, and the $k=2,3$ cases don't change. (Given (SA2), (SA1) and (SA1') are equivalent anyway, since $X\setminus\varnothing=X$ and $X\setminus X=\varnothing$.)

3. *Countable intersections instead of unions.* If (SA3) is phrased with countable intersections, use $\phi_3'((A_n))=\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n$ (for $X$ itself, the empty intersection isn't needed here, since the index set is $\mathbb N\neq\varnothing$). The $k=3$ argument is again verbatim.

In each case the $\sigma$-algebras on $X$ are exactly the magmas of sets for a suitable explicit family of operations on $\mathcal P(X)$. So the concept of $\sigma$-algebra is an instance of a magma of sets.
